teaching_goal:
This course aims to provide graduate students with a comprehensive understanding of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) — a field that combines reinforcement learning (RL) and deep learning (DL) to enable intelligent agents to learn complex behaviors through interaction with environments.
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
1.	Understand the theoretical foundations of reinforcement learning, including Markov decision processes, Bellman equations, policy evaluation, and value iteration.
2.	Apply deep learning techniques (e.g., convolutional and recurrent neural networks) to approximate value functions and policies.
3.	Implement and analyze key DRL algorithms such as DQN, DDPG, A3C, PPO, and SAC.
4.	Experiment with real-world or simulated environments using frameworks such as OpenAI Gym, PyTorch, or TensorFlow.
5.	Critically evaluate current research papers and identify emerging trends and open challenges in DRL.
6.	Design and implement a mini-project or research proposal demonstrating the application of DRL to a specific problem domain (e.g., robotics, games, control systems, or autonomous decision-making).
teaching_content:
This course provides a rigorous and comprehensive introduction to Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) — the interdisciplinary field at the intersection of machine learning, control theory, and artificial intelligence.
Students will explore how intelligent agents learn to make sequential decisions through interaction with dynamic environments using reward-driven learning frameworks.
The course covers fundamental topics in reinforcement learning, including Markov decision processes (MDPs), value-based and policy-based methods, temporal-difference learning, and exploration–exploitation trade-offs. Building on these foundations, students will study deep neural architectures that enable DRL agents to operate in high-dimensional, complex environments.
Through lectures, hands-on coding assignments, and research-oriented projects, students will gain both theoretical understanding and practical implementation skills. Real-world applications — such as robotics, autonomous driving, game playing (e.g., AlphaGo), and resource optimization — will be discussed to illustrate the transformative potential of DRL.

teaching_goal: The goal of privacy preserving data analysis is to retrieve useful information from big data while preserving users’ privacy. This course will provide a comprehensive introduction to the concepts and methods of privacy-preserving data analysis.
teaching_content:
This course will introduce four key concepts:
1. Data Anonymization: This involves techniques such as k-anonymity and l-diversity, which are employed to prevent linking attacks and homogeneity attacks.
2. Differential Privacy: This is a mathematical framework for releasing statistical information about datasets while protecting the privacy of individual data subjects, which protects individual’s privacy by injecting carefully calibrated noise into the released data.
3. Cryptography: This involves techniques like secure multiparty computation, which allows multiple organizations or individuals to collaborate on computations without disclosing their own data.
4. Federated Learning: This is a decentralized learning approach that enables participants to keep their data local while collaboratively training a machine learning model, balancing privacy protection with model performance.

name_zh: AI代理系統之設計與開發
teaching_goal:
With the advances in computer vision, speech recognition, and large language models, we can now equip computers with perception and generative ability. Large language models brained Agents in particular have been a key breakthrough, allowing Agentic AI to reason its world through natural language and leverage broad knowledge to make smarter decisions.
This course aims to explore the theoretical foundations of Agentic AI and the platforms and tools for developing AI agents. The focus will be guiding students in creating autonomous agents capable of operating independently, making decisions in complex environments, and completing sophisticated tasks.

Learning Objectives
Upon completing this course, students will be able to:
Understand the fundamental principles and architecture of Agentic AI systems.
Design and implement essential AI agents using modern frameworks and tools.
Consider ethical and safety aspects in AI agent design.
Evaluate the performance and limitations of Agentic AI systems.
Assess the challenges AI agents face when interacting in real-world environments.

Prerequisites
Programming background (Python)
Familiarity with basic artificial intelligence concepts
Fundamental knowledge of machine learning and neural networks
teaching_content:
This hands-on course focuses on developing autonomous AI agents with practical applications, emphasizing web interaction, multi-agent systems, memory management, and human-in-the-loop learning. Students will progressively build an agent system through four interconnected assignments and a final project.
Weeks 1: Course Introduction
● Introduction to agency in AI systems
● Historical development of autonomous agents
● Agent architectures and frameworks
● Core components: perception, reasoning, and action
● Practical: Building a simple rule-based agent
● Readings: Agentic AI concepts, Chatbots vs. Copilots vs. AI Agents
Weeks 2-4: Assignment 1 - Reflexive Web Agent with Tools Use (15%)
● Language models brained agents
● Prompt engineering for agency
● Tool use and API interaction
● LLM Reasoning: Chain-of-Thoughts, Tree-of-Thoughts
● Schema-guided task-oriented dialog systems
● Vision Language Models models
Technical Focus
● Prompt Engineering: Assign specialized roles and pre-built and custom tools to agents
● Planning algorithm
● Basic web interaction patterns
● Selenium
● Web Crawling
Weeks 5-7: Assignment 2 - Self-Reflection via MultiAgent Collaboration (15%)
● Agent communication and coordination framework: Collaborative and competitive agents
● Decision-making under uncertainty
● Reinforcement learning for agent behavior
● Self-Reflection mechanism
● Evaluation of task result for decision-making
● Guardrails: consider governance in design, development and deployment stages
Technical Focus
● Break down the tasks, goals, and tools and assign to multiple AI agents for better performance
● LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI
Weeks 8-10: Assignment 3 - Agents with Memory Recall via RAG (15%)
● Memory management systems: Provide agents with short-term, long-term, and shared memory
● Goal representation and task decomposition
● Information retrieval based on embedding
● Retrieval augmented generation
● Object reference resolution
Technical Focus
● RAG architecture design
● Query optimization
Week 11: Midterm Examination (15%)
Weeks 12-14: Human in the Loop Reinforcement Learning (15%)
● Human in the Loop Interaction
● Experience recording
● Memory persistence
● Task decomposition and Hierarchical architectures
● Adaptive behavior patterns Technical Focus
● Instruction-guided learning implementation
● RAG optimization for learned behaviors
Weeks 15-18: Final Project (25%)
● Integrate all previous assignments to a real-world environment
● Define environment and actions, e.g. LINE APP, Windows OS, or Smart Home APP
● Guardrails: Effectively handle errors, hallucinations, and infinite loops
Technical Focus
● Complete agent system integration
● Environment-specific adaptations
● Comprehensive documentation
● Performance optimization
